levels.title: The Young Couple
levels.story: Maria and Jose just got married. They are a happy young couple excited about their future together. Before starting a family, they visit a health center to learn the basics of family planning. The friendly nurse smiles and says: 'Knowledge is the first step to a healthy family. Let's see what you already know!'

questions.question: What does 'family planning' mean?
options: Planning a family vacation
Deciding when and how many children to have
Planning family finances only
Arranging family events
questions.answer: Deciding when and how many children to have
questions.explanation: Family planning means making informed choices about if, when, and how many children to have, using contraception and other methods.

questions.question: Which of the following is a natural method of family planning?
options: Birth control pills
Condoms
Calendar/Rhythm method
Intrauterine Device (IUD)
questions.explanation: The calendar or rhythm method is a natural family planning method where couples track the menstrual cycle to avoid pregnancy during fertile days.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of contraception?
options: To cure sexually transmitted infections
To prevent unwanted pregnancy
To increase fertility
To regulate hormones only
questions.explanation: Contraception is used to prevent unintended pregnancy, giving couples control over when they start or grow their family.

questions.question: Who should be involved in family planning decisions?
options: Only the woman
Only the man
Both partners together
Only the doctor
questions.explanation: Family planning is a shared responsibility. Both partners should communicate and decide together for the best outcomes.

questions.question: At what age is a woman generally considered to have the highest fertility?
options: Teens (13-19)
Early to mid-20s
Late 30s
Early 40s
questions.explanation: A woman's fertility is generally highest in her early to mid-20s and gradually declines with age, especially after 35.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Using contraception means you do not want children at all.
options: MYTH — Contraception is about timing, not rejecting children
FACT — People who use contraception never want kids
MYTH — Only unmarried people use contraception
FACT — Contraception permanently ends fertility
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Contraception is about timing, not rejecting children
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Contraception simply helps couples decide WHEN to have children, not whether to have them at all. Many people use contraception to space births responsibly.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The pill causes permanent infertility.
options: MYTH — Fertility usually returns within 1-3 months of stopping
FACT — The pill permanently damages the reproductive system
MYTH — The pill works for 5 years after stopping
FACT — Fertility never returns after long-term pill use
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Fertility usually returns within 1-3 months of stopping
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. For most women, fertility returns within 1 to 3 months after stopping the pill. The pill does not cause permanent infertility.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Family planning is only a woman's responsibility.
options: MYTH — Family planning is a shared responsibility for both partners
FACT — Only women need to worry about family planning
MYTH — Men have no role in contraception
FACT — Family planning laws require only women to act
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Family planning is a shared responsibility for both partners
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Family planning is the shared responsibility of both partners. Men can use condoms, vasectomy, or support their partner's chosen method.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: You cannot get pregnant the first time you have sex.
options: MYTH — Pregnancy is possible any time ovulation occurs
FACT — First-time sex never results in pregnancy
MYTH — The body needs time before becoming fertile
FACT — Pregnancy requires multiple encounters
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Pregnancy is possible any time ovulation occurs
myth_busting.explanation: This is a dangerous myth. Pregnancy is absolutely possible the first time. If ovulation has occurred, conception can happen regardless of prior sexual experience.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Natural family planning methods like the rhythm method are 100% effective.
options: MYTH — Natural methods are only 76-88% effective with typical use
FACT — The rhythm method never fails if followed correctly
MYTH — Natural methods are more effective than condoms
FACT — No method of family planning ever fails
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Natural methods are only 76-88% effective with typical use
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Natural methods like the rhythm method have typical-use failure rates of 12-24%. They require consistent and careful tracking to be effective.

scenario.question: Maria tells her friend: 'Jose and I are newlyweds and want to wait 2 years before having children.' Her friend suggests just using withdrawal. What should Maria do?
options: Accept the advice — withdrawal is fully reliable
Consult a health worker for a more reliable contraceptive method
Use nothing since they are married
Try the rhythm method alone
scenario.answer: Consult a health worker for a more reliable contraceptive method
scenario.explanation: Withdrawal (pull-out) has a typical-use failure rate of about 22%. Maria and Jose should visit a health center to choose a reliable method that fits their needs and lifestyle.

scenario.question: A couple decides to use the calendar method but the woman has irregular cycles. What is the most important next step?
options: Continue using only the calendar method
Use a backup method or switch to a more reliable option
Ignore cycle irregularity — it does not matter
Stop using any method since cycles are irregular
scenario.answer: Use a backup method or switch to a more reliable option
scenario.explanation: The calendar method depends on regular cycles to predict fertile days. Irregular cycles make this method very unreliable. A backup method or alternative should be used.

scenario.question: Jose says he does not want to be involved in family planning decisions. What is the best way for Maria to handle this?
options: Accept his refusal and decide alone
Discuss the importance of shared responsibility and seek couples counseling if needed
Stop using any contraception
Ask only her parents for advice
scenario.answer: Discuss the importance of shared responsibility and seek couples counseling if needed
scenario.explanation: Family planning works best as a team decision. Maria should talk to Jose about shared responsibility. A health counselor or community health worker can help facilitate the conversation.

scenario.question: A 22-year-old woman wants to start family planning but is nervous about side effects of hormonal methods. What is the best first step?
options: Avoid all contraception until she feels ready
Visit a health professional to discuss all options and their side effect profiles
Use only herbal remedies
Ask friends for advice only
scenario.answer: Visit a health professional to discuss all options and their side effect profiles
scenario.explanation: A licensed health professional can explain all available methods, both hormonal and non-hormonal, and help the woman choose one that matches her health profile and comfort level.

scenario.question: A newly married couple believes they should have children immediately because 'that is what marriage is for.' Their health worker disagrees. Why might the health worker recommend waiting?
options: The health worker is overstepping boundaries
Couples should wait to allow physical, emotional, and financial readiness
Early pregnancy is medically encouraged for all couples
Waiting is only recommended for older couples
scenario.answer: Couples should wait to allow physical, emotional, and financial readiness
scenario.explanation: Health workers often recommend allowing time after marriage to establish stability. Physical, emotional, and financial readiness contribute to better outcomes for both parents and child.

levels.title: The Health Center Visit
levels.story: Ana is a 24-year-old mother of one child. She returns to the health center for her postnatal check-up. The midwife explains that proper spacing between pregnancies is very important for both mother and baby. Ana listens carefully, eager to learn more so she can make the best choices for her growing family.

questions.question: What is the recommended minimum birth spacing between pregnancies?
options: 6 months
12 months
At least 2 years
5 years
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization recommends waiting at least 2 years (24 months) after a live birth before the next pregnancy to reduce health risks.

questions.question: Which of these is a barrier method of contraception?
options: Birth control pill
Condom
Hormonal injection
IUD
questions.explanation: A condom is a barrier method — it physically prevents sperm from reaching the egg. It also helps protect against STIs.

questions.question: Breastfeeding can act as a natural contraceptive method. What is this called?
options: Natural Cycle Method
Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM)
Rhythm Method
Billings Method
questions.explanation: LAM relies on exclusive breastfeeding to suppress ovulation. It is effective only if the baby is under 6 months, the mother is exclusively breastfeeding, and menstruation has not returned.

questions.question: Which vitamin is most important for women planning to get pregnant?
options: Vitamin C
Vitamin D
Folic Acid (Vitamin B9)
Vitamin K
questions.explanation: Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects in the baby. Women planning pregnancy are advised to take 400mcg daily before conception and during early pregnancy.

questions.question: What does prenatal care mean?
options: Care given after delivery
Care given to newborns
Medical care during pregnancy
Care given to elderly parents
questions.explanation: Prenatal care is the healthcare a woman receives during pregnancy to monitor her health and the development of the baby.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Breastfeeding fully protects a mother from getting pregnant.
options: MYTH — LAM only works under 3 strict conditions
FACT — Breastfeeding is 100% effective contraception
MYTH — You cannot get pregnant at all while breastfeeding
FACT — Breastfeeding replaces all other contraception
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — LAM only works under 3 strict conditions
myth_busting.explanation: Breastfeeding as contraception (LAM) only works if: the baby is under 6 months old, breastfeeding is exclusive, and menstruation has not returned. Without all three, pregnancy is possible.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Short birth spacing (less than 18 months) has no health impact on the mother or baby.
options: MYTH — Short spacing increases risks for both mother and infant
FACT — Spacing does not affect maternal or infant health
MYTH — The body recovers fully after 6 months
FACT — Only older mothers need to worry about birth spacing
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Short spacing increases risks for both mother and infant
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Short interpregnancy intervals increase the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, maternal anemia, and uterine rupture (especially after C-section).

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The condom is the least effective method of contraception.
options: MYTH — With correct and consistent use, condoms are 97-98% effective
FACT — Condoms fail most of the time
MYTH — Condoms only work 50% of the time
FACT — Condoms are not considered a real contraceptive method
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — With correct and consistent use, condoms are 97-98% effective
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. When used correctly and consistently, condoms are 97-98% effective. They also uniquely provide dual protection against both pregnancy and STIs.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: You do not need prenatal care if you feel healthy during pregnancy.
options: MYTH — Many pregnancy complications show no symptoms early on
FACT — Prenatal care is only needed if you feel sick
MYTH — Home remedies can replace clinical prenatal care
FACT — Only high-risk mothers need prenatal visits
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Many pregnancy complications show no symptoms early on
myth_busting.explanation: This is a dangerous myth. Many serious conditions like hypertension, gestational diabetes, and fetal abnormalities have no obvious symptoms. Regular prenatal visits are essential for all pregnancies.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: IUDs are only suitable for women who have already had children.
options: MYTH — IUDs are safe and effective for most women regardless of childbirth history
FACT — IUDs can only be used after giving birth
MYTH — IUDs cause permanent damage in young women
FACT — IUDs reduce future fertility permanently
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — IUDs are safe and effective for most women regardless of childbirth history
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Modern guidelines confirm IUDs are appropriate for most women including adolescents and those who have never been pregnant, subject to clinical assessment.

scenario.question: Ana just gave birth 3 months ago and is exclusively breastfeeding. She asks the midwife if she needs contraception. What should the midwife advise?
options: No — she is fully protected by breastfeeding indefinitely
Yes — LAM only works reliably for up to 6 months and she should plan ahead
No — new mothers cannot get pregnant for a year
Yes — she should immediately use an IUD with no other options
scenario.answer: Yes — LAM only works reliably for up to 6 months and she should plan ahead
scenario.explanation: LAM is effective for up to 6 months with exclusive breastfeeding and no return of menstruation. Ana should begin planning her next contraceptive method before the 6-month mark.

scenario.question: A mother who had a cesarean section 10 months ago wants to get pregnant again. Her doctor advises waiting. Why?
options: The doctor wants her to lose weight first
WHO recommends at least 24 months after C-section to allow uterine scar healing
It is only a cultural preference with no medical basis
She must complete a nutrition program first
scenario.answer: WHO recommends at least 24 months after C-section to allow uterine scar healing
scenario.explanation: WHO recommends a minimum of 24 months after a cesarean section before the next pregnancy. The uterine scar needs adequate time to heal to reduce the risk of rupture.

scenario.question: Ana's neighbor says she stopped taking folic acid once her pregnancy test was positive. Is this the right time to start or stop?
options: Correct — folic acid is only needed before pregnancy
Wrong — folic acid should be started before conception and continued through early pregnancy
Correct — folic acid is only for high-risk pregnancies
Wrong — folic acid is only needed in the third trimester
scenario.answer: Wrong — folic acid should be started before conception and continued through early pregnancy
scenario.explanation: Folic acid should ideally be started at least 1 month BEFORE conception and continued through the first trimester. Neural tube formation happens very early, before many women know they are pregnant.

scenario.question: A postnatal patient says she wants to use contraception but her husband is against it. What is the health worker's best response?
options: Tell her to obey her husband's wishes
Invite both partners for counseling and explain the health benefits of birth spacing
Prescribe contraception secretly without telling the husband
Tell her to wait until her husband agrees
scenario.answer: Invite both partners for counseling and explain the health benefits of birth spacing
scenario.explanation: The health worker should respect patient autonomy while addressing the husband's concerns. Couples counseling often resolves conflicts by explaining the medical and family benefits of planned birth spacing.

scenario.question: A new mother is using a condom as her only contraceptive method postpartum. She reports occasional inconsistent use. What should the health worker recommend?
options: Condoms are fine even with inconsistent use
Add a more reliable long-term method such as an IUD or implant alongside condoms
Stop using contraception since inconsistency makes it pointless
Switch to the rhythm method instead
scenario.answer: Add a more reliable long-term method such as an IUD or implant alongside condoms
scenario.explanation: Inconsistent condom use significantly raises failure risk. Adding a reliable long-acting method (like an IUD or implant) while continuing condoms provides dual protection — against both pregnancy and STIs.

levels.title: The Community Seminar
levels.story: A community health worker named Lito is conducting a family planning seminar in a small village. Many couples and young adults have gathered, curious but also with many questions. Lito opens with a serious message: 'Understanding your options can save lives and build stronger families. Are you ready to go deeper?' The room goes quiet with anticipation.

questions.question: What is an Intrauterine Device (IUD)?
options: A daily oral pill to prevent pregnancy
A small device inserted into the uterus to prevent pregnancy
A hormonal patch worn on the skin
A surgical procedure for permanent contraception
questions.answer: A small device inserted into the uterus to prevent pregnancy
questions.explanation: An IUD is a small T-shaped device placed inside the uterus by a healthcare provider. It can be hormonal or copper-based and provides long-term contraception.

questions.question: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
options: Birth control pills
IUD
Condoms
Hormonal implant
questions.explanation: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that provides dual protection — preventing both pregnancy and STIs, including HIV.

questions.question: What is meant by 'unmet need for family planning'?
options: Women who want more children
Women who want to avoid pregnancy but are not using contraception
Couples who cannot afford to have children
Men who refuse to discuss family planning
questions.answer: Women who want to avoid pregnancy but are not using contraception
questions.explanation: Unmet need refers to women who are sexually active, want to delay or stop childbearing, but are not using any form of contraception.

questions.question: What is the typical effectiveness rate of birth control pills when used correctly?
options: Around 70%
Around 80%
Around 91-99%
questions.explanation: With perfect use, birth control pills are about 99% effective. With typical use (occasional missed pills), effectiveness is around 91%.

questions.question: Which of the following is a permanent method of contraception for men?
options: Vasectomy
Tubal ligation
Hormonal implant
Male condom
questions.explanation: A vasectomy is a surgical procedure that cuts or blocks the vas deferens, preventing sperm from being released. It is considered permanent contraception for men.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The IUD causes abortion because it prevents a fertilized egg from implanting.
options: MYTH — IUDs primarily prevent fertilization, not implantation
FACT — IUDs always work by destroying fertilized eggs
MYTH — IUDs have no effect on fertilization
FACT — All IUDs are medically classified as abortifacients
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — IUDs primarily prevent fertilization, not implantation
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. The primary mechanism of IUDs is to prevent fertilization — copper IUDs via sperm toxicity, hormonal IUDs via cervical mucus thickening and ovulation suppression. Most medical bodies do not classify IUDs as abortifacients.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Contraceptive implants make women gain a lot of weight.
options: MYTH — Studies show no significant average weight gain with implants
FACT — All women gain 10+ kg from hormonal implants
MYTH — Weight gain is the main reason implants are removed
FACT — Implants cause weight gain in all users
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Studies show no significant average weight gain with implants
myth_busting.explanation: Clinical studies show no statistically significant average weight gain associated with contraceptive implants. Some individuals may notice minor changes, but this is not a universal effect.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: A vasectomy reduces a man's sexual drive and performance.
options: MYTH — Vasectomy has no effect on testosterone, libido, or sexual function
FACT — Vasectomy causes hormonal changes that reduce desire
MYTH — Vasectomy changes the appearance of ejaculate
FACT — Men become infertile and lose interest in sex after vasectomy
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Vasectomy has no effect on testosterone, libido, or sexual function
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. A vasectomy only blocks the vas deferens. It does not affect testosterone production, sexual drive, erection quality, or orgasm. The only change is that semen no longer contains sperm.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The pill protects against sexually transmitted infections.
options: MYTH — Only condoms provide STI protection; the pill does not
FACT — The pill creates a barrier against bacteria and viruses
MYTH — All hormonal methods protect against STIs
FACT — The pill reduces STI risk by 50%
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Only condoms provide STI protection; the pill does not
myth_busting.explanation: This is a critical myth to bust. Birth control pills prevent pregnancy by hormonal means but provide zero protection against STIs including HIV, chlamydia, and gonorrhea. Only condoms provide STI protection.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Communities with high unmet need for family planning simply do not want contraception.
options: MYTH — Unmet need is driven by barriers like access, cost, and misinformation
FACT — People in underserved areas prefer large families
MYTH — Lack of contraception use means lack of interest
FACT — Unmet need means there are too many contraceptive options
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Unmet need is driven by barriers like access, cost, and misinformation
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Unmet need is driven by barriers including geographic inaccessibility, cost, fear of side effects, partner or community opposition, cultural beliefs, and misinformation — not lack of desire.

scenario.question: During the seminar, a woman says she stopped using the pill because she heard it causes cancer. How should Lito respond?
options: Validate her fear and tell her to avoid all hormonal methods
Explain that while there are small risk increases for some cancers, the pill also reduces risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer
Tell her that the pill is completely risk-free
Ignore her concern and move on
scenario.answer: Explain that while there are small risk increases for some cancers, the pill also reduces risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer
scenario.explanation: A balanced, evidence-based response is needed. Combined oral contraceptives slightly increase breast and cervical cancer risk but significantly reduce ovarian and endometrial cancer risk. The overall benefit-risk profile depends on individual health factors.

scenario.question: A village couple wants a long-term method since they have already had 3 children and want no more. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Continue with condoms only
Recommend a long-acting reversible method like an IUD or implant, or discuss permanent options
Tell them to use abstinence
Suggest the rhythm method only
scenario.answer: Recommend a long-acting reversible method like an IUD or implant, or discuss permanent options
scenario.explanation: For couples who have completed their family, long-acting reversible contraceptives (IUD, implant) are highly effective with no daily effort. If they are certain about no more children, permanent methods (tubal ligation, vasectomy) can be discussed.

scenario.question: A seminar attendee asks: 'If condoms are the only method that prevents STIs, why do many people not use them?' What is Lito's best answer?
options: Because people do not care about STIs
Because of cultural stigma, reduced sensation claims, cost, and lack of availability
Because condoms are too complicated to use
Because STIs are no longer a concern
scenario.answer: Because of cultural stigma, reduced sensation claims, cost, and lack of availability
scenario.explanation: Barriers to condom use include cultural or religious stigma, the myth that condoms reduce pleasure, cost, limited access, and lack of negotiation power especially for women. Addressing these barriers is a key part of community health education.

scenario.question: A man in the seminar says he supports family planning but believes it is only for his wife to manage. What should Lito emphasize?
options: Agree — women are biologically responsible for contraception
Male involvement improves contraceptive use, communication, and overall family health outcomes
Tell him to stay quiet since he has no role
Suggest he attend a different seminar
scenario.answer: Male involvement improves contraceptive use, communication, and overall family health outcomes
scenario.explanation: Research consistently shows that male involvement in family planning leads to better contraceptive adherence, reduced unintended pregnancies, and improved maternal and child health outcomes. Men can use condoms, vasectomy, or actively support their partner.

scenario.question: A couple asks if they should use dual protection even though the wife is already on the pill. What should Lito advise?
options: No — the pill is enough
Yes — if there is any STI risk, condoms should be added alongside the pill
No — using two methods at once is dangerous
Yes — but only if the husband agrees
scenario.answer: Yes — if there is any STI risk, condoms should be added alongside the pill
scenario.explanation: The pill prevents pregnancy but not STIs. Dual protection (pill + condom) is recommended for couples where either partner has STI risk factors. This provides protection against both unintended pregnancy and infection.

levels.title: The Teenage Dilemma
levels.story: In a high school health class, teacher Ms. Santos faces a room full of teenagers with big questions about reproductive health. Many of them are confused by myths they've heard from friends. Ms. Santos speaks firmly: 'The truth about your reproductive health matters more than rumors. Let's separate fact from fiction — your future depends on it.'

questions.question: TRUE or FALSE: A woman can get pregnant during her period.
options: False — it is impossible
True — it is possible, though less likely
Only if it is her first period
Only in older women
questions.answer: True — it is possible, though less likely
questions.explanation: While less likely, pregnancy during menstruation is possible because sperm can survive up to 5 days, and some women have short cycles with early ovulation.

questions.question: What is adolescent reproductive health?
options: Health issues only affecting teenage boys
The physical, mental, and social well-being related to reproduction in young people aged 10-24
A program for married teenagers
Nutrition advice for teenagers
questions.answer: The physical, mental, and social well-being related to reproduction in young people aged 10-24
questions.explanation: Adolescent reproductive health encompasses the physical, emotional, and social aspects of sexual and reproductive health for young people aged 10-24.

questions.question: What is a common risk of teenage pregnancy?
options: Faster recovery after birth
Higher likelihood of completing education
Higher risks of maternal and infant complications
No significant health differences
questions.answer: Higher risks of maternal and infant complications
questions.explanation: Teenage pregnancies carry higher risks including preeclampsia, anemia, premature birth, low birth weight, and higher maternal and infant mortality.

questions.question: Which hormone triggers ovulation in women?
options: Estrogen
Progesterone
Luteinizing Hormone (LH)
Testosterone
questions.explanation: A surge in Luteinizing Hormone (LH) triggers the release of a mature egg from the ovary — this process is called ovulation.

questions.question: What is the fertile window in a typical 28-day menstrual cycle?
options: Days 1-5
Days 10-17
Days 20-25
Days 25-28
questions.explanation: In a 28-day cycle, ovulation typically occurs around day 14. The fertile window spans about 5 days before and 1-2 days after ovulation — approximately days 10-17.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Teenagers cannot access family planning services without parental consent.
options: MYTH — Adolescents have the right to confidential reproductive health services in many countries
FACT — All minors must have parental approval for any health service
MYTH — Health workers must always call parents when treating teens
FACT — Teens are legally barred from health centers alone
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Adolescents have the right to confidential reproductive health services in many countries
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. In many countries including the Philippines, adolescents have the right to access reproductive health information and services confidentially. Parental consent is not always legally required.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Talking to teenagers about contraception encourages early sexual activity.
options: MYTH — Research shows sex education delays sexual debut and promotes safer behaviour
FACT — Teaching about contraception leads directly to more teen sex
MYTH — Ignorance is the best protection for teenagers
FACT — Schools that teach sex ed have higher teen pregnancy rates
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Research shows sex education delays sexual debut and promotes safer behaviour
myth_busting.explanation: This is a well-documented myth. Multiple studies show that comprehensive sex education actually delays the age of first sexual activity and increases safer sexual behavior when it does occur.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: A girl cannot get pregnant if it is her first time having sex.
options: MYTH — Pregnancy is possible any time ovulation has occurred, including the first time
FACT — The body is not fertile during first sexual experience
MYTH — The hymen prevents pregnancy on the first encounter
FACT — First-time sex cannot result in fertilization
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Pregnancy is possible any time ovulation has occurred, including the first time
myth_busting.explanation: This is a very dangerous myth. Pregnancy can absolutely occur during a first sexual encounter if ovulation has taken place. There is no biological protection tied to sexual experience level.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Teenage pregnancy only affects girls from poor or uneducated families.
options: MYTH — Teenage pregnancy affects young people across all socioeconomic groups
FACT — Only girls without education get pregnant as teenagers
MYTH — Wealth fully protects against teenage pregnancy
FACT — Teen pregnancy is a problem only in rural areas
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Teenage pregnancy affects young people across all socioeconomic groups
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Teenage pregnancy occurs across all socioeconomic backgrounds, educational levels, and communities. It is influenced by access to information, support systems, peer pressure, and relationship dynamics — not just poverty.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Emergency contraception (the morning-after pill) is the same as an abortion pill.
options: MYTH — Emergency contraception prevents fertilization; it does not terminate an existing pregnancy
FACT — Both pills work in exactly the same way
MYTH — Emergency contraception works by removing a fertilized egg
FACT — Morning-after pills and abortion pills have identical mechanisms
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Emergency contraception prevents fertilization; it does not terminate an existing pregnancy
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Emergency contraception (like levonorgestrel) works primarily by delaying or preventing ovulation, stopping fertilization before it occurs. It is not effective if implantation has already happened and is not an abortion pill.

scenario.question: A 16-year-old girl confides in Ms. Santos that she is sexually active and worried about pregnancy. She is afraid to tell her parents. What should Ms. Santos do?
options: Immediately call her parents without her consent
Provide confidential counseling and information about reproductive health services available to adolescents
Tell her to stop being sexually active and send her home
Ignore the situation to avoid controversy
scenario.answer: Provide confidential counseling and information about reproductive health services available to adolescents
scenario.explanation: Ms. Santos should provide a safe, non-judgmental space. Adolescents have rights to confidential reproductive health counseling. The teacher should guide her toward appropriate health services and support.

scenario.question: Two male students in the class say that contraception is 'not their problem.' How should Ms. Santos address this?
options: Agree and focus only on female students
Explain that male responsibility in contraception is medically, socially, and ethically important
Ask the boys to leave the class
Skip the topic to avoid conflict
scenario.answer: Explain that male responsibility in contraception is medically, socially, and ethically important
scenario.explanation: Ms. Santos should directly challenge this misconception. Male partners play a critical role in contraceptive decisions. Condoms, vasectomy, and active communication are male contributions to family planning and sexual health.

scenario.question: A student says her friend took emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected sex and it did not work. Why might this have happened?
options: Emergency contraception never works
Emergency contraception is most effective within 72 hours and effectiveness drops after 72 hours
The brand she used was fake
Emergency contraception only works for married women
scenario.answer: Emergency contraception is most effective within 72 hours and effectiveness drops after 72 hours
scenario.explanation: Levonorgestrel-based emergency contraception is most effective within 72 hours (3 days) of unprotected sex. By day 4-5, effectiveness is significantly reduced. A copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception up to 5 days after.

scenario.question: A 17-year-old student asks: 'If I am on the pill, do I still need to use a condom?' What is the correct answer?
options: No — the pill protects against everything
Yes — condoms should be added if there is any risk of STIs, since the pill only prevents pregnancy
No — using both together is dangerous
Yes — you must always use both methods with no exceptions
scenario.answer: Yes — condoms should be added if there is any risk of STIs, since the pill only prevents pregnancy
scenario.explanation: The pill is highly effective at preventing pregnancy but provides zero STI protection. If there is any risk of STI exposure, a condom should also be used. This dual protection approach is strongly recommended for sexually active adolescents.

scenario.question: A student reports that her 15-year-old classmate is already 3 months pregnant and hiding it from everyone. What is the priority health concern?
options: The classmate should be expelled from school
She needs immediate access to prenatal care regardless of the circumstances
She should be encouraged to hide the pregnancy longer
The situation is not the school's concern
scenario.answer: She needs immediate access to prenatal care regardless of the circumstances
scenario.explanation: Teenage pregnancy carries elevated risks of complications. The immediate health priority is accessing prenatal care to monitor both mother and fetus. Schools and health workers should support, not stigmatize, pregnant adolescents.

levels.title: The Midwife's Challenge
levels.story: You are a newly licensed midwife assigned to a remote rural health unit. Your senior midwife, Ma'am Reyes, hands you a thick case file and says with a serious look: 'These families are counting on you. You need to know more than the basics — you need expert-level knowledge. Lives depend on the advice you give.' Your training is about to be truly tested.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of action of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs)?
options: They destroy sperm in the cervix
They thicken cervical mucus only
They suppress ovulation by preventing LH and FSH surges
They prevent implantation only
questions.answer: They suppress ovulation by preventing LH and FSH surges
questions.explanation: COCPs primarily work by suppressing the LH and FSH surges needed for ovulation. They also thicken cervical mucus and thin the endometrial lining as secondary mechanisms.

questions.question: What is the key eligibility criterion for the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) to be effective?
options: Baby must be under 12 months, any breastfeeding
Baby under 6 months, exclusively breastfed, and menses not resumed
Mother is taking iron supplements
Baby under 1 year and partially breastfed
questions.answer: Baby under 6 months, exclusively breastfed, and menses not resumed
questions.explanation: LAM requires all three conditions: infant less than 6 months old, exclusively breastfeeding (no supplemental feeds), and maternal amenorrhea (no return of menstruation).

questions.question: Which condition is classified as a Category 4 (absolute contraindication) for combined hormonal contraceptives under WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria?
options: Mild hypertension
History of migraines without aura
Breastfeeding a 3-month-old infant
History of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
questions.explanation: History of DVT is WHO MEC Category 4, meaning combined hormonal contraceptives must not be used as the estrogen component significantly increases the risk of recurrent thromboembolism.

questions.question: What is 'postpartum family planning' primarily focused on?
options: Planning the next pregnancy immediately after birth
Preventing unintended pregnancy in the first 12 months after delivery
Nutritional planning for the newborn
Scheduling postnatal doctor visits
questions.answer: Preventing unintended pregnancy in the first 12 months after delivery
questions.explanation: Postpartum family planning focuses on helping women avoid unintended pregnancy during the first 12 months after birth, protecting both maternal health and birth spacing.

questions.question: According to WHO, what is the recommended interpregnancy interval after a cesarean section?
options: At least 6 months
At least 12 months
At least 18 months
At least 24 months
questions.explanation: WHO recommends a minimum interpregnancy interval of 24 months after a cesarean section to allow adequate uterine scar healing and reduce risks of uterine rupture.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The progestin-only pill (minipill) is safe for breastfeeding mothers.
options: FACT — The minipill does not contain estrogen and is safe for postpartum breastfeeding women
MYTH — All oral contraceptives reduce breast milk supply
MYTH — The minipill affects infant hormone levels significantly
FACT — All pills are equally safe during breastfeeding
myth_busting.answer: FACT — The minipill does not contain estrogen and is safe for postpartum breastfeeding women
myth_busting.explanation: This is a FACT. Unlike combined pills, the progestin-only pill contains no estrogen and does not significantly affect breast milk supply or infant health. It is a WHO-recommended option for breastfeeding women after 6 weeks postpartum.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Hormonal implants must be replaced every year.
options: MYTH — Most implants last 3-5 years depending on the type
FACT — All implants need annual replacement
MYTH — Implants expire after exactly 12 months
FACT — Implants stop working after 18 months
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Most implants last 3-5 years depending on the type
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Single-rod implants (e.g., Implanon/Nexplanon) are effective for up to 3 years. Some newer types last up to 5 years. Annual replacement is not required.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: A woman with controlled hypertension cannot use any form of hormonal contraception.
options: MYTH — Progestin-only methods are generally acceptable even with controlled hypertension
FACT — All hormonal methods are banned for any hypertensive patient
MYTH — Hypertension automatically means WHO MEC Category 4 for all methods
FACT — Only combined pills are restricted for hypertensive women
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Progestin-only methods are generally acceptable even with controlled hypertension
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. WHO MEC distinguishes between method types and hypertension severity. Combined hormonal contraceptives may be restricted (Category 3-4) depending on severity, but progestin-only pills, implants, and IUDs are generally Category 1-2 for controlled hypertension.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: After a vasectomy, a man is immediately sterile.
options: MYTH — It takes several weeks and a semen analysis to confirm sterility after vasectomy
FACT — Vasectomy makes a man instantly and completely sterile
MYTH — Sterility is confirmed 24 hours after vasectomy
FACT — A vasectomy takes effect the moment the procedure ends
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — It takes several weeks and a semen analysis to confirm sterility after vasectomy
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. After a vasectomy, sperm already in the reproductive tract must be cleared. A semen analysis (typically after 20 ejaculations or 3 months) is required to confirm azoospermia (no sperm). Another method must be used in the interim.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Tubal ligation is reversible in all cases.
options: MYTH — Tubal ligation should be considered permanent; reversal is not guaranteed
FACT — Tubal ligation can always be fully reversed
MYTH — Reversal is simple and has a 100% success rate
FACT — All women who want reversal can achieve pregnancy
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Tubal ligation should be considered permanent; reversal is not guaranteed
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. While tubal ligation reversal surgery exists, success rates vary widely (30-90%) depending on the method used, age, and time elapsed. It should be counseled as a permanent method.

scenario.question: A 30-year-old patient with a history of DVT requests combined oral contraceptives. What is the correct clinical response?
options: Prescribe them — DVT history is only a relative contraindication
Decline and offer progestin-only or non-hormonal alternatives — DVT is WHO MEC Category 4 for COCs
Prescribe a low-dose option as a compromise
Ask her to consult a cardiologist first then prescribe
scenario.answer: Decline and offer progestin-only or non-hormonal alternatives — DVT is WHO MEC Category 4 for COCs
scenario.explanation: History of DVT is an absolute contraindication (WHO MEC Category 4) for combined hormonal contraceptives due to the thrombogenic effect of estrogen. The midwife must offer safer alternatives such as progestin-only pills, copper IUD, or implants.

scenario.question: A new mother who is 8 weeks postpartum is exclusively breastfeeding and wants to start contraception. She wants an oral method. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs)
Progestin-only pill (minipill) started at 6 weeks postpartum
Emergency contraceptive pills
No oral method is safe postpartum
scenario.answer: Progestin-only pill (minipill) started at 6 weeks postpartum
scenario.explanation: COCPs are generally not recommended before 6 months postpartum in breastfeeding women (WHO MEC Category 4 before 6 weeks, Category 3 from 6 weeks to 6 months). The progestin-only pill is safe from 6 weeks postpartum and does not affect milk supply.

scenario.question: A rural patient with limited literacy comes alone for contraceptive counseling. She is afraid of injections and surgical procedures. What is the best approach?
options: Prescribe the most effective method regardless of her fears
Use visual aids and simple language to explain options, and collaboratively choose a method she is comfortable with
Tell her only injections and implants are available
Send her to a specialist in the city
scenario.answer: Use visual aids and simple language to explain options, and collaboratively choose a method she is comfortable with
scenario.explanation: Person-centered counseling requires adapting communication to the patient's literacy level and respecting her fears and preferences. A method the patient is comfortable with and will consistently use is more effective than a theoretically superior method she refuses or misuses.

scenario.question: A patient 4 months after C-section wants to start using a copper IUD. Her last pregnancy was uncomplicated except for the surgical delivery. Is this appropriate?
options: No — copper IUDs are permanently contraindicated after C-section
Yes — after complete uterine healing, a copper IUD is appropriate and WHO supports this
No — she must wait 5 years after C-section
Yes — but she must be on antibiotics for 6 months first
scenario.answer: Yes — after complete uterine healing, a copper IUD is appropriate and WHO supports this
scenario.explanation: WHO MEC classifies IUD insertion at 4+ weeks postpartum (including after C-section) as Category 1-2. By 4 months, the uterus has adequately healed. A copper IUD is a highly effective long-term option with no hormonal effects.

scenario.question: During home visits, a midwife notices a woman has 5 children under age 6, is anemic, and has no contraception. What is the priority action?
options: Advise diet changes only
Provide immediate contraceptive counseling focused on long-acting methods and refer for anemia treatment
Tell her to have no more children without offering options
Document the case and return next month
scenario.answer: Provide immediate contraceptive counseling focused on long-acting methods and refer for anemia treatment
scenario.explanation: This is a high-priority situation involving both reproductive health and nutritional risk. The midwife should provide counseling on reliable long-acting methods (IUD, implant) to prevent further rapid pregnancies while also addressing the anemia through referral and supplementation.

levels.title: The Expert Counselor
levels.story: You are the most experienced family planning counselor in the region. A difficult case arrives: a woman with multiple health conditions seeking contraceptive advice, and a community with deeply rooted misconceptions. The Department of Health has sent you to resolve this complex situation. Your supervisor says gravely: 'Only someone with mastery of family planning can handle this. This is the final test of your expertise.'

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman who smokes more than 15 cigarettes per day wants to use combined oral contraceptives. What is the WHO MEC classification?
options: Category 1 — no restriction
Category 2 — advantages generally outweigh risks
Category 3 — risks generally outweigh advantages
Category 4 — unacceptable health risk, must not use
questions.answer: Category 4 — unacceptable health risk, must not use
questions.explanation: A woman aged 35+ who smokes ≥15 cigarettes/day is WHO MEC Category 4 for combined hormonal contraceptives due to significantly elevated cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk.

questions.question: What is the copper IUD's secondary mechanism that makes it effective as emergency contraception?
options: It suppresses ovulation within 72 hours
Copper ions are spermicidal and may prevent fertilization or implantation
It releases levonorgestrel to prevent fertilization
It creates a hormonal barrier in the cervix
questions.answer: Copper ions are spermicidal and may prevent fertilization or implantation
questions.explanation: The copper IUD works primarily by releasing copper ions that are toxic to sperm (spermicidal), impairing sperm motility and viability. It may also prevent implantation. It can be used as emergency contraception up to 5 days after unprotected sex.

questions.question: In the context of family planning counseling, what does the GATHER model stand for?
options: Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Explain, Return
Guide, Assess, Treat, Help, Evaluate, Refer
Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Educate, Request
Guide, Address, Talk, Handle, Educate, Return
questions.answer: Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Explain, Return
questions.explanation: The GATHER model is a family planning counseling framework: Greet the client, Ask about their needs, Tell them about options, Help them choose, Explain how to use the method, and Return/follow-up visit.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'dual protection' in family planning?
options: Using two different hormonal methods simultaneously
Using condoms to prevent both STIs and unintended pregnancy, along with another method
Protecting both partners using separate methods
Using contraception during and after pregnancy
questions.answer: Using condoms to prevent both STIs and unintended pregnancy, along with another method
questions.explanation: Dual protection means using condoms (to prevent STI/HIV transmission) together with another reliable contraceptive method (for pregnancy prevention), providing protection against both risks.

questions.question: What is the global unmet need for family planning primarily attributed to?
options: Lack of desire for contraception
Barriers including access, cost, misinformation, partner opposition, and fear of side effects
Government policies banning contraception
Lack of contraceptive technology
questions.answer: Barriers including access, cost, misinformation, partner opposition, and fear of side effects
questions.explanation: The global unmet need (affecting ~218 million women) is driven by multiple barriers: geographic access, cost, social and cultural norms, partner or family opposition, misinformation, and fear of side effects — not lack of desire.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Family planning programs are a form of population control imposed on developing nations.
options: MYTH — Ethical FP programs are rights-based and empower individuals to make their own choices
FACT — All family planning programs are designed to reduce population in poor countries
MYTH — International health organizations have no interest in individual reproductive rights
FACT — FP programs always set quotas for how many children families can have
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — Ethical FP programs are rights-based and empower individuals to make their own choices
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. Ethical family planning programs, as defined by WHO, UNFPA, and the Reproductive Health Law, are fundamentally rights-based. They empower individuals and couples to decide freely the number and spacing of their children — they do not coerce or impose limits.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Hormonal contraceptives cause depression in all users.
options: MYTH — While some users report mood changes, the evidence for universal depression is not established
FACT — All hormonal contraceptives clinically cause depression
MYTH — Hormonal methods have zero effect on mental health
FACT — All women should be screened for depression before using any hormonal method
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — While some users report mood changes, the evidence for universal depression is not established
myth_busting.explanation: Research on hormonal contraceptives and mood is mixed. Some studies suggest a small increased risk of depression in certain users, particularly adolescents. However, universal causation has not been established. Counseling should include discussion of potential mood effects.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The copper IUD has no hormonal effects and is suitable for women who cannot use hormonal methods.
options: FACT — The copper IUD is non-hormonal and is a strong option for women with hormonal contraindications
MYTH — All IUDs release hormones
MYTH — Copper IUDs affect estrogen levels
FACT — Copper IUDs and hormonal IUDs work identically
myth_busting.answer: FACT — The copper IUD is non-hormonal and is a strong option for women with hormonal contraindications
myth_busting.explanation: This is a FACT. The copper IUD works entirely through copper ion toxicity to sperm — no hormones are involved. It is an excellent option for women with conditions like DVT, breast cancer history, or other WHO MEC Category 4 conditions for hormonal methods.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) are more cost-effective than short-acting methods over time.
options: FACT — LARCs have higher upfront cost but lower long-term cost per year of protection
MYTH — Daily pills are always cheaper than LARCs
MYTH — LARCs cost the same as daily pills over 5 years
FACT — Only governments can afford LARCs; they are not practical for individuals
myth_busting.answer: FACT — LARCs have higher upfront cost but lower long-term cost per year of protection
myth_busting.explanation: This is a FACT. While IUDs and implants cost more upfront, they are significantly more cost-effective over their lifespan (3-10 years) compared to daily pills, monthly injections, or condoms. Health economists consistently rank LARCs as the most cost-effective contraceptive options.

myth_busting.question: MYTH or FACT: The GATHER counseling model is outdated and no longer used in modern family planning.
options: MYTH — GATHER remains a widely taught and applied framework in reproductive health counseling globally
FACT — GATHER has been replaced by newer digital tools
MYTH — GATHER is only used in the Philippines
FACT — Modern counseling has abandoned all structured frameworks
myth_busting.answer: MYTH — GATHER remains a widely taught and applied framework in reproductive health counseling globally
myth_busting.explanation: This is a myth. The GATHER model (Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Explain, Return) continues to be widely used and taught in family planning training globally. It provides a structured, client-centered approach that improves counseling quality and client satisfaction.

scenario.question: A 38-year-old woman with migraine with aura, who smokes, requests combined oral contraceptives. How should the expert counselor respond?
options: Prescribe low-dose COCs as a compromise
Decline — both migraine with aura and smoking at 35+ are independent WHO MEC Category 4 conditions for COCs
Offer COCs but monitor her closely
Tell her only natural methods are safe for her
scenario.answer: Decline — both migraine with aura and smoking at 35+ are independent WHO MEC Category 4 conditions for COCs
scenario.explanation: Migraine with aura and smoking aged 35+ are each independently WHO MEC Category 4 for combined hormonal contraceptives due to markedly elevated stroke risk. The counselor must firmly decline and offer safe alternatives such as progestin-only methods or copper IUD.

scenario.question: A community requests family planning education but community leaders insist contraception is against their beliefs. How should the counselor approach this?
options: Cancel the program and leave
Respect cultural values, engage leaders, and focus on information and voluntary choice — not coercion
Force the program through without community consent
Report the community leaders to health authorities
scenario.answer: Respect cultural values, engage leaders, and focus on information and voluntary choice — not coercion
scenario.explanation: Ethical family planning counseling respects autonomy and community values. The counselor should engage community leaders in dialogue, frame family planning as a rights-based health service, and ensure all participation is voluntary. Coercion is a violation of reproductive rights.

scenario.question: A woman asks about using the copper IUD for emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected sex. She is not interested in continuing it long-term. Is this appropriate?
options: No — copper IUDs cannot be used for emergency contraception
Yes — the copper IUD is effective up to 5 days after unprotected sex and can be removed after the next period
No — she must use it for at least 1 year
Yes — but only if she agrees to keep it for 5 years
scenario.answer: Yes — the copper IUD is effective up to 5 days after unprotected sex and can be removed after the next period
scenario.explanation: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception available (>99% effective up to 5 days). It can be removed after the next menstrual period if the woman does not wish to continue long-term use. She should be counseled on this option.

scenario.question: During a GATHER counseling session, a client seems embarrassed and gives vague answers about her reproductive history. What is the counselor's priority at this stage?
options: Skip the assessment and go straight to prescribing
Build trust and rapport — make the client feel safe before proceeding with detailed questions
Tell the client that honesty is required by law
End the session and reschedule
scenario.answer: Build trust and rapport — make the client feel safe before proceeding with detailed questions
scenario.explanation: The GATHER model begins with Greet — establishing rapport and a non-judgmental environment. Clients who feel safe provide more accurate reproductive histories, enabling better counseling. Rushing past this step compromises the quality of the entire encounter.

scenario.question: A couple asks for the most effective reversible contraceptive method available. What should the expert recommend?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pills (91-99% typical use)
Male condom (85% typical use)
Intrauterine device or contraceptive implant (>99% typical and perfect use)
Fertility awareness methods (76-88% typical use)
scenario.answer: Intrauterine device or contraceptive implant (>99% typical and perfect use)
scenario.explanation: IUDs and contraceptive implants are the most effective reversible contraceptive methods available, with over 99% effectiveness for both typical and perfect use. Unlike pills or condoms, they require no daily action and have minimal user-error failure.
